title: JESUS TOLD ONE MAN, “DON’T TELL ANYONE.” THEN HE TOLD ANOTHER, “GO TELL EVERYONE.” WHY?
paragraphs: JESUS TOLD ONE MAN, “DON’T TELL ANYONE.” THEN HE TOLD ANOTHER, “GO TELL EVERYONE.” WHY?

Two broken men. Two extraordinary miracles. Two seemingly opposite commands from the same Savior. And hidden in the difference is a truth that could change the way you understand your testimony, your obedience, and what Jesus is asking of you right now.
Scripture: Mark 1:40–45; Mark 5:1–20
There is something in the Gospel of Mark that most Christians have read without ever stopping long enough to question.
Jesus healed a man suffering from leprosy and gave him a stern warning.
Don't tell anyone.
Later, Jesus delivered a man who had been living among tombs, tormented by unclean spirits, and gave him an entirely different command.
Go home. Tell everyone what the Lord has done for you.
Wait.
The same Jesus?
The same compassion?
The same supernatural power?
Yet one man was told to remain silent, while another was sent out to speak.
Was Jesus contradicting Himself?
Was one miracle more important than the other?
Was one man's testimony more valuable?
Or is there something happening beneath these two encounters that reveals how deeply Jesus understands the human heart, the timing of God's purposes, and the cost of following Him?
Because here is the question that might reach further into your life than you expect:
What if the greatest issue isn't whether you are telling people about Jesus, but whether you are actually listening to Him?
Stay with that question.
Because before this is over, we need to talk about something uncomfortable.
It is possible to be genuinely grateful for what Jesus has done and still disobey what Jesus has said.
And sometimes, the thing we call devotion is actually our own desire wearing religious clothing.
That is not an accusation against every enthusiastic believer.
It is a warning worth examining in our own hearts.
And the two men in Mark's Gospel help us understand why.
Picture the first man.
He is standing somewhere near the edges of ordinary human life.
We do not know his name.
We do not know how long he has suffered.
We do not know whether he has a wife who misses him, children who remember his voice, or a mother who still prays for him.
Scripture does not give us those details, and we should not invent them as facts.
But we do know something about the world in which he lived.

Under the purity regulations of Leviticus 13–14, certain serious skin conditions could result in a person being declared ceremonially unclean. Those affected could be required to live apart from the community until their condition was properly examined and their cleansing recognized.
The Greek word used in Mark 1:40 is λεπρός (lepros), traditionally translated as “leper.”

It is important to understand that the biblical category of lepra was broader than what modern medicine identifies as Hansen's disease. We cannot diagnose this man's exact medical condition from Mark's account.
But whatever his particular disease, his suffering was real.
His exclusion was real.
And his longing to be restored was real.
Imagine living with a condition that does not merely affect your body but can also determine whether you are permitted to participate in ordinary community life.
Imagine watching people gather while you remain outside.
Imagine wanting to be seen as a human being rather than as a condition.
And then imagine hearing that Jesus of Nazareth is nearby.
The man approaches Him.
He kneels.
And he says something astonishing.
“If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.” — Mark 1:40, KJV
Notice what he does not say.
He does not question Jesus' power.
He questions whether Jesus is willing.
That is a painfully familiar kind of faith.
Some of us have never doubted that God is powerful.
We have doubted whether His compassion could possibly reach someone like us.
We believe He can forgive sins.
But what about ours?
We believe He restores broken people.
But what about someone who has failed repeatedly?
We believe He loves the world.
But sometimes, in the quietest moments, we wonder whether that love truly includes us.
The man says, in effect:
Lord, I know You are able.
But are You willing?
And Jesus answers with more than words.
Mark 1:41 records that Jesus stretched out His hand and touched him.
Think about that.
The man came seeking cleansing.
Jesus responded with a touch.
The Gospel does not say how long the man had gone without human contact. We should not pretend to know.
But in a society where his condition carried serious purity implications, the significance of that touch is extraordinary.
Jesus did not recoil from him.
He reached toward him.
The Greek words of Jesus are breathtaking in their simplicity:
θέλω, καθαρίσθητι
Thelō, katharisthēti.
“I will; be thou clean.” — Mark 1:41, KJV
The first word, thelō, expresses willingness: “I am willing.”
The second, katharisthēti, is an imperative meaning “be cleansed.”
Jesus did not merely possess the power to cleanse.
He exercised that power in compassion.
And immediately, according to Mark 1:42, the man's condition departed, and he was cleansed.
The man who had approached Jesus with uncertainty about His willingness now stood as living evidence of His mercy.
You would expect the next command to be obvious.
Go tell everybody.
Tell the village.
Tell your family.
Tell every person who ever avoided you.
But Jesus says something unexpected.
“See thou say nothing to any man: but go thy way, shew thyself to the priest, and offer for thy cleansing those things which Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them.” — Mark 1:44, KJV
Silence.
At least for now.
And obedience to the prescribed process.
Why?
Because Jesus was not merely performing a spectacle.
He was restoring a man in a way that acknowledged the requirements of the Law of Moses.

Leviticus 14 describes priestly examination and offerings connected with cleansing. The priest did not create the healing; his role included examining the condition and carrying out the prescribed procedures for restoration.
Jesus directed the man toward that process.
He was not telling him that his miracle was unimportant.
He was giving him a specific next step.
And the timing mattered.
Throughout Mark's Gospel, Jesus repeatedly resists allowing public excitement, misunderstanding, or premature claims about His identity to dictate the course of His mission.
Scholars often discuss this pattern under the expression “Messianic secret.”
But we must be careful.
That scholarly term does not explain every command of silence by itself, and Scripture does not explicitly tell us every motive behind Jesus' instruction in this particular encounter.
What Mark does show us is the consequence when the man acts differently.
Mark 1:45 says he went out and began to proclaim the matter widely.
And then comes the detail that should make us stop.
Jesus could no longer openly enter a town in the same way.
He remained outside in more deserted places, while people continued coming to Him from everywhere.
Do you see the painful irony?
The man who had experienced exclusion could now move forward into restored life.
But Jesus, because of the publicity surrounding the miracle, was now unable to enter towns openly.
That does not mean Jesus became ceremonially unclean or that the man's actions defeated God's sovereign purposes.
Mark is describing a practical consequence for Jesus' public ministry.
The man's announcement contributed to a situation in which Jesus' movements became more restricted.
And here is the uncomfortable truth.
Something can be completely true and still be shared in a way that disregards God's instruction.
The man's healing was real.
His excitement was understandable.
His testimony was powerful.
But Mark records that he did not follow the command Jesus had given him.
We are not told every motive in his heart.
We should not confidently declare that he was arrogant, rebellious, or ungrateful.
But we can say that his actions differed from Jesus' explicit instruction.
And that distinction matters.
Because many of us understand the excitement of wanting to do something big for God.
We want to announce.
We want to act.
We want to prove how grateful we are.
But sometimes Jesus is asking for something quieter.
Make the apology.
Tell the truth.
Return what you took.
End the deception.
Honor the commitment.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
Obey the instruction already made clear in Scripture.
We can become so eager to do something impressive for God that we neglect something simple He has already commanded.
And perhaps that is where this first encounter begins to expose us.
Not every open door is permission.
Not every good intention is obedience.
Not every religious activity is surrender.
Sometimes the most faithful testimony is not what comes out of your mouth.
It is what changes in your life.
But then Mark takes us to another man.
And everything seems to reverse.
This man is not suffering from a skin condition.
He is living among tombs.
Mark 5 describes a man possessed by unclean spirits, crying out and injuring himself with stones.
Others had attempted to restrain him with chains and shackles.
The restraints had failed.
No one had been able to subdue him.
Try to imagine the loneliness of that existence.
Not the sensational version we sometimes see in religious entertainment.
The human reality.
A man in terrible bondage.
A man separated from ordinary community life.
A man whose suffering had become frightening to those around him.

Scripture does not identify his condition as an ordinary mental illness, and we must not equate mental illness with demonic possession. Mark presents this particular event as an encounter involving unclean spirits.
The distinction matters because people living with psychiatric conditions deserve compassion, appropriate care, and freedom from spiritual stigma.
But within Mark's account, the man's bondage is devastating.
And then Jesus arrives.
The unclean spirits recognize His authority.
They cannot negotiate as equals with Him.
They cannot overpower Him.
They cannot prevent Him from delivering the man.
The narrative includes the spirits' request to enter a herd of pigs and the destruction of that herd.
And when the people from the surrounding region come to see what has happened, they discover something remarkable.
Mark 5:15 describes the formerly possessed man as sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
The man who had lived among tombs is now sitting before Jesus.
The man others could not restrain is no longer described as violent or tormented.
The man whose life had been consumed by bondage is now experiencing deliverance.
What a scene.
Not because it is dramatic.
Because it is personal.
There is a human being here whose life has changed.
And yet the response of the surrounding people is startling.
They become afraid.
And they ask Jesus to leave their region.
The One who has just demonstrated authority over evil is not welcomed by everyone.
That detail should humble us.
A miracle can confront people with the power of God without automatically producing faith.
A person can witness something extraordinary and still want Jesus at a distance.
And perhaps that is not as unfamiliar as we would like to believe.
We want Jesus to solve what hurts.
But do we welcome His authority over what we refuse to surrender?
We want peace.
But do we want the Prince of Peace to rule our decisions?
We want freedom from consequences.
But do we want freedom from sin?
We want a Savior.
But do we want a Lord?
Then comes the moment that connects this story to the first.
As Jesus prepares to leave, the delivered man begs to go with Him.
It is a beautiful request.
After everything he has endured, who could blame him?
The One who freed him is leaving.
Of course he wants to stay close.
But Jesus does not permit him to come.
Instead, He says:
“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.” — Mark 5:19, KJV
In Greek, the command begins:
Ὕπαγε εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου πρὸς τοὺς σούς
Hypage eis ton oikon sou pros tous sous.
“Go to your home, to your own people.”
And the command continues:
καὶ ἀπάγγειλον αὐτοῖς
kai apangeilon autois.
“And report to them.”
The Greek verb apangeilon carries the sense of reporting or announcing something.
Jesus gives the man a mission.
Not an imaginary mission.
Not a glamorous one.
Not the mission the man requested.
A mission rooted in his own community.
Go home.
Tell your people.
Tell them what the Lord has done.
Tell them about His mercy.
Now consider the difference.
The first man wanted to spread the news and was told not to.
The second man wanted to accompany Jesus and was told to go spread the news.
Both men had experienced extraordinary mercy. Both received instructions that required surrendering their preferred response.
And that is where the two stories meet.
Jesus was not contradicting Himself.
He was directing different people in different circumstances according to the purposes of His ministry.
In Mark 1, the public spread of the healing report interfered with Jesus' ability to enter towns openly.
In Mark 5, Jesus was departing from a predominantly Gentile region associated with the Decapolis, and He commissioned the delivered man to tell his own people what the Lord had done.
The contexts were different.
The immediate instructions were different.
But the authority behind both commands was the same.
Jesus was Lord in both situations.
And obedience to Him was the appropriate response in both.
Notice something else.
The second man obeyed.
Mark 5:20 says:
“And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel.” — KJV
Jesus told him to announce what the Lord had done.
And Mark says he announced what Jesus had done.
That wording is significant.
Mark's narrative closely associates the Lord's mercy with the work of Jesus.
We should not force more into the verse than it explicitly states, but the connection contributes to Mark's unfolding presentation of Jesus' extraordinary authority and identity.
And the man's testimony reaches beyond his immediate household.
He begins proclaiming throughout the Decapolis.
The man who once lived among tombs becomes a witness to mercy.
He does not need a sophisticated theological vocabulary.
He does not need a stage.
He does not need an impressive religious résumé.
He has something real to tell.
He knows what Jesus has done for him.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
Your testimony does not have to sound like someone else's.
You do not need to exaggerate your suffering to make God's grace look powerful.
You do not need to invent a dramatic past.
You do not need to pretend that every problem has disappeared.
You can simply tell the truth.
I was lost, and Christ called me to repentance.
I was guilty, and I found mercy at the cross.
I was proud, and God's Word humbled me.
I am still learning to trust Him.
I am still fighting against sin.
I still need His grace every single day.
A truthful testimony does not become weak because it is unfinished.
And a Christian life does not become meaningless because it is ordinary.
But there is a deeper truth in these two stories that we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus did not give either man the right to define discipleship on his own terms.
One man could not turn gratitude into permission to disregard a command.
The other could not turn love for Jesus into permission to abandon the assignment Jesus gave him.
Both encounters confront the same question.
Will you follow Jesus only when His instruction agrees with your desire?
Or will you follow Him because He is Lord?
That question becomes especially painful when obedience is costly.
Sometimes we want to speak, but wisdom requires restraint.
Sometimes we want to remain silent, but faithfulness requires us to speak.
Sometimes we want to leave our circumstances, but God calls us to serve faithfully where we are.
Sometimes we want to remain comfortable, but obedience requires a difficult step.
We should not assume that every personal impression is a direct command from God. Scripture calls us to test what we believe, seek wisdom, and remain faithful to what God has revealed.
But when His Word is clear, our task is not to negotiate with it.
It is to respond in faith.
And that brings us to the heart of the Gospel.
Because if this article ended with “Just obey better,” it would leave us with a burden we cannot carry on our own.
The Gospel is not the announcement that disciplined people can earn God's acceptance by perfect obedience.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Our disobedience is not a small problem.
Our pride is not harmless.
Our attempts to justify ourselves cannot make us righteous before a holy God.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
That includes the outwardly religious.
The secretly ashamed.
The person with a scandalous past.
And the person whose sins have remained hidden behind a respectable reputation.
We do not all carry the same stories.
But we all need the same Savior.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve our public image.
He came to reconcile sinners to God through His death and resurrection.
He lived without sin.
He gave Himself on the cross.
He bore the judgment our sins deserved.
And He rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our publicity, our donations, our religious activity, or our promises to do better.
It is received through God's grace in Jesus Christ, through faith that turns to Him in repentance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
And Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
Grace gives obedience its proper place.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
We obey because the Savior who loved us has called us to follow Him.
This is why the theme of scandal and grace is more than a beautiful phrase.
Scandal is not always something the whole world discovers.
Sometimes scandal lives behind a locked screen.
Sometimes it hides in a dishonest transaction.
Sometimes it grows inside resentment that nobody sees.
Sometimes it is the private habit we keep defending.
Sometimes it is a religious reputation covering a heart that has drifted far from God.
But grace does not mean God pretends our sin is harmless.
Grace means Christ offers forgiveness and new life to people who cannot save themselves.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
And transformation is not merely learning to look respectable.
It is the continuing work of God in a life surrendered to Christ.
That is why we say:
Not because Jesus erases every earthly consequence.
Not because every relationship is automatically restored.
Not because Christians never struggle again.
But because sin and shame do not have to possess the final word over the person who belongs to Christ.
The cross is greater than our attempts to save ourselves.
The resurrection is greater than the grave.
And the grace of Jesus is greater than the false identity our failures try to give us.
There is something especially moving about the two men in Mark.
One needed cleansing.
The other needed deliverance.
Both encountered Jesus.
And both were given a next step.
Perhaps that is what you need to consider today.
Not a spectacular plan for the next ten years.
Not an impressive speech about what you will someday accomplish.
Just the next faithful step.
For someone, it may be confessing a sin they have spent years hiding.
For someone else, it may be forgiving a person while still maintaining necessary and healthy boundaries.
For another, it may be seeking help, returning to prayer, opening Scripture again, or finally telling a trusted Christian that they are struggling.
For someone, the next step may be to stop talking about their faith as though it were merely a public identity and begin living it in private.
And for someone else, it may be to stop hiding the hope they have found in Jesus because they are afraid of what people will think.
The same Savior who told one man to be silent and another to speak still teaches His people that faithfulness is not measured by noise.
It is measured by trust expressed through obedience.
But there is one more detail I do not want you to miss.
In Mark 5, the delivered man wanted to be physically near Jesus.
He begged to accompany Him.
And Jesus sent him home.
Think about the tenderness and difficulty of that moment.
The man's desire to remain near his Deliverer was understandable.
But Jesus had a purpose for him beyond the boat.
His own people needed to hear about mercy.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Sometimes we imagine that serving Jesus means escaping ordinary life.
Leaving behind difficult relationships.
Finding a bigger audience.
Being recognized.
Doing something people will applaud.
Yet the Lord may call us to begin with the people who know us best.
The family member who remembers our worst season.
The friend who knows how stubborn we used to be.
The person who watched us fail.
The neighbor who has heard our excuses.
Not to impress them.
Not to demand that they believe us immediately.
Not to use our testimony to pressure them.
But to live honestly before them and, when appropriate, tell them what Christ has done.
Because the people who knew our old patterns may also be the people who most clearly notice genuine change.
And genuine change takes more than a dramatic announcement.
It takes time.
Humility.
Repentance.
Consistency.
The daily dependence of a believer who knows that without Christ, he cannot produce lasting spiritual fruit.
Maybe that is why Jesus' command in Mark 5 is so powerful.
Go home.
Not because home is easy.
But because home matters.
Tell your own people.
Not because everyone will respond positively.
But because mercy is worth bearing witness to.
Tell them what the Lord has done.
Not what you have accomplished by your own strength.
Not how spiritually superior you have become.
Tell them about His mercy.
His mercy.
That is the center of the testimony.
And it must remain the center of Gospel Warrior too.
Not our name.
Not our reach.
Jesus Christ.
If this message has uncovered something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond honestly.
Not with a polished religious sentence.
Not with words designed to impress anyone.
Just truth.
You do not need to reveal private details, expose another person, or share anything that would put you at risk.
Sometimes the simple words “Christ is still working in me” are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And please, do not let this message end with you if someone in your life genuinely needs its encouragement.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because someone among your friends may be silently wrestling with the same question.
Am I really following Jesus?
Or am I only following Him when it is convenient?
There may come a day when you need to return to the difference between enthusiasm and obedience.
When you need to remember that God's instructions are not always identical for every person or every situation.
When you need to remind yourself that the most important question is not, “What are other Christians doing?”
But, “What does faithfulness to Jesus require of me?”
If you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I invite you to stay connected.
Bring your friends, your family, the believers who need strengthening, and even those who are still exploring what Christianity truly teaches.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where difficult questions are welcomed, where repentance is not treated as a dirty word, and where grace is never separated from truth.
And if you want to go deeper than a single article, there is another invitation I would like you to consider.

Gospel Warrior is building and expanding a discipleship ministry centered on Jesus Christ, biblical teaching, spiritual encouragement, and resources that help people grow in their understanding of God's Word.

That library exists because we believe biblical nourishment should be accessible to people who are hungry to grow in Christ, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian learning materials.
But maintaining, developing, and expanding a ministry like this requires ongoing support.
It is voluntary financial support that helps sustain the work and contributes toward expanding the resources and outreach we hope to provide.
But I want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches us to honor the Lord with our resources, support faithful ministry, care for people in need, and give willingly rather than under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That matters.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and the needs of people around you deserve thoughtful consideration as you make decisions about giving.
Those items are simply an additional expression of appreciation.
They are not the heart of the invitation.
The heart is discipleship.
The heart is making biblical resources available.
The heart is helping more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Read.
Pray.
Use the free resources.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
The Gospel does not belong to those who can pay for access.
Thank you for considering being part of that mission.
But before you leave, return with me to the two men.
One had suffered under a condition that separated him from ordinary community life.
The other had lived among tombs, bound by unclean spirits.
One was told not to spread the news.
The other was told to announce what the Lord had done.
Different commands.
Different circumstances.
The same Jesus.
And in both encounters, the miracle was never supposed to become more important than the One who performed it.
That is the danger we must remember.
We can become fascinated with what Jesus gives and forget to surrender to who Jesus is.
We can celebrate His mercy while resisting His authority.
We can speak beautifully about grace while refusing to repent.
We can build an entire religious identity around telling people about Jesus and still neglect the quiet obedience of actually following Him.
But He calls us to something deeper.
Not a performance.
Not a brand.
Not a reputation.
A life surrendered to Him.
If you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ, do not mistake admiration for saving faith.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
You do not need to make yourself worthy before approaching Him.
You need the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And if you already belong to Christ but have wandered, do not use yesterday's failure as an excuse to remain far from Him today.
Confess your sin.
Receive His forgiveness.
Return to His Word.
Walk in the light.
Keep following Him.
Because the question is not whether your past was too scandalous for grace.
The question is whether you will trust the Savior whose grace is sufficient to forgive and transform sinners.
One man heard, “Say nothing.”
Another heard, “Go home and tell.”
And perhaps the most important words for us are not either command in isolation.
Perhaps they are the words of Mary at Cana, spoken to the servants in John 2:5:
“Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.” — KJV
That is not a command to invent private revelations or ignore the teaching of Scripture.
It is a beautiful expression of the posture every disciple should have toward Christ.
Listen to Him.
Trust Him.
Obey Him.
When He calls you to speak, speak truthfully and lovingly.
When wisdom requires silence, do not confuse restraint with cowardice.
When He calls you to repent, stop defending what He calls sin.
When He calls you to love, do not wait until the other person has earned your kindness.
When He calls you to bear witness, do not be ashamed of His Gospel.
And when you stumble, remember that your hope is not in a flawless record of obedience.
Your hope is in Jesus Christ, the crucified and risen Lord.
Am I more interested in being known as someone who talks about Jesus, or in becoming someone who truly follows Him?
Sit with that.
Let Scripture search your heart.
Then take the next step that obedience requires.
Because one day, the most beautiful part of your testimony may not be how loudly you announced that Jesus changed your life.
It may be how faithfully you walked with Him after the excitement of the miracle had passed.
The deepest evidence that you have encountered Jesus is not merely that you have a story to tell, but that His grace is teaching you to live a different one.
